analysis.one_liner: Requires banks to refund customers who were tricked or coerced into sending money to scammers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2024 with no cosponsors, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received any further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, if a scammer steals your card number and drains your account, your bank generally has to reimburse you — but if a scammer tricks or pressures you into sending the money yourself (a fake romance, a phony bank fraud call, a bogus investment), the transfer counts as "authorized" and you are usually out of luck. This bill rewrites the Electronic Fund Transfer Act so a transfer you were deceived or coerced into approving gets the same protection as an unauthorized one: your bank must reimburse you, and the loss is then split evenly between your bank and the bank that received the money. It also expands the definition of a bank "error" to include consumer mistakes and money frozen in inaccessible accounts.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who lose money to payment scams — fake bank-fraud calls, romance scams, bogus investment pitches, text-message phishing — where they personally authorized the transfer because they were deceived or coerced. Under current rules those transfers are treated as authorized and the consumer typically eats the loss; the bill would instead require their bank to reimburse them and then split the loss with the receiving institution. Consumers with funds frozen in inaccessible accounts, and consumers charged for goods never delivered or accepted, would also gain stronger dispute rights.

how_it_helps.text: Scam victims who authorized a transfer because they were deceived or coerced would get the same reimbursement rights today given to victims of outright theft, including the limited-liability schedule in the Electronic Fund Transfer Act.
The bank holding the victim's account must reimburse the consumer, and the loss is then split evenly with the bank that received the money, so neither side can simply blame the other.

It adds errors to the legal definition of "error" — including mistakes by consumers and money stuck in frozen or inaccessible accounts — so consumers can force an investigation of those situations too.
It clarifies that nothing in the bill limits the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's authority to add further protections.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit unions, and payment platforms, which would bear the cost of reimbursing scam-induced transfers and share liability with the receiving institution; they could pass some of that cost to customers through fees or tighter fraud controls, and the rules could add friction to legitimate transfers.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes banks and credit unions cover scam-induced transfers they could not detect, and makes the sending and receiving institutions split the loss evenly; some of that cost could come back to customers through higher fees or tighter transaction limits.

"Fraudulently induced" is a broad category that covers transfers the consumer personally authorized, so banks and the CFPB would have to sort genuine scam victims from disputed transactions, disputed claims, and transfers made with fraudulent intent, which the bill carves out but which can be difficult to identify in practice.

The bill relies heavily on new rulemaking by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to define which institutions share liability, adding a layer of regulatory interpretation on top of the statutory change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: people tricked by impersonation, romance, and investment scams would get their money back instead of being told the loss was their fault, and liability would push the sending and receiving banks to invest in fraud detection rather than treat each other as blameless pass-throughs. The costs are also real: a broad definition of "fraudulently induced" is hard to adjudicate, banks would absorb large new fraud losses that they may partly pass on through fees or tighter transaction friction, and the CFPB would need substantial rulemaking to sort out who pays when more than two institutions touch a transfer. On balance the bill shifts losses from scam victims to the payment system, which is where many experts argue they belong, but it was written quickly, introduced in the final months of a Congress with no cosponsors, and was never tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2024 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which took no action on it before the term ended, so it never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Introduced in the House on August 2, 2024 and referred to the Committee on Financial Services the same day.
The action history shows no further steps: no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
No other House member signed on as a cosponsor.

Under the bill, a transfer a consumer was tricked or coerced into approving would be treated like an unauthorized transfer: the consumer's bank must reimburse the loss, then shares that loss evenly with the bank that received the money.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and payment platforms keep the existing rules, under which a customer tricked into approving a payment is generally not reimbursed; scam victims remain responsible for losses from fraudulently induced transfers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks and payment platforms; scam victims left unprotected

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on August 2, 2024 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress — no markup, no committee vote, no report to the floor.

against.name: Banking and payments industry
against.role: Banks, credit unions, and payment platforms that would bear new fraud-loss liability
against.what_they_did: Industry groups have consistently opposed treating scam-induced, consumer-authorized transfers like unauthorized ones, because it would shift large fraud losses onto financial institutions — the same position banks took in public comments on the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's similar proposal.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no record of how parties lined up; the bill was introduced by the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee but drew zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: They would have to reimburse scam victims whose transfers the consumer authorized, and split fraud losses with the receiving institution — a large new cost under the current rules, under which consumers who were tricked into approving a payment usually eat the loss. For ordinary people, bank-held fraud losses replace unrecoverable personal losses.

industries.industry: Payment networks and P2P payment platforms
industries.note: Under the expanded definition, platforms and institutions that facilitate transfers of scammed funds could be pulled into shared liability, including institutions the CFPB identifies as materially supporting transfers. Today, fast payment rails such as instant P2P transfers are a major channel for scams because recoveries are rare.

industries.industry: Scam victims and consumers with inaccessible or disputed funds
industries.note: Not an industry, but the group the bill is built around: people who lost money to payment scams, and people with money frozen in accounts they cannot reach, would gain a legal right to reimbursement and investigation.
